Rouen
roo-AHN
n. (the Norman capital whose Reformed cloth trade was broken by the Revocation and carried to Norwich and Spitalfields)
French Rouen, from Latin Rotomagus, the market of the wheel or of Roto; the city stands on the Seine below Paris.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Rouen is the Norman capital whose Protestant population was large, industrial and in the end exported. The city held one of the biggest Reformed congregations in France, concentrated among its cloth merchants, dyers, weavers and printers; it was taken by the Reformed in 1562 and retaken by the crown with a sack, and it suffered prison massacres in September 1572 after the Paris killings. Under the Edict of Nantes it had a temple outside the walls at Quevilly and a share in the Chambre de l'Edit, the mixed court at Paris that heard Protestant cases. The Revocation of 1685 fell on Rouen as an industrial event. Emigration was forbidden on pain of the galleys, and the Protestants of Rouen left anyway in thousands, taking their skills with them: the new-draperies of Norwich, the silk weaving of Spitalfields in London, and workshops in Holland and Brandenburg were built on French artisans, many of them from Normandy, and the trade of Rouen did not recover for generations. Elie Benoist, pastor at Alencon, wrote the history of the whole business from exile in Delft. The dictionary enters Rouen because the Revocation is usually counted in souls and should also be counted in looms, since the king who drove them out impoverished himself to do it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a draper as one who deals in cloth; a loom as a frame for weaving; emigration as removal from one country to another; and a galley as a vessel rowed by convicts.

expand to see more

DRAPER, n. One who sells cloths; a dealer in cloths; as a linen draper or woolen draper.

LOOM, n. A frame or machine of wood or other material, in which a weaver works threads into cloth.

EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.

GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel navigated with sails and oars, often rowed by criminals condemned to it.

ARTISAN, n. One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman.

Key Scripture

Act 18:3 — "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers."

1Th 4:11 — "And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;"

Act 8:1 — "And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles."

Act 11:19 — "Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only."

Modern Corruption

Norman capital whose large Reformed artisan population was massacred in 1572 and, after the Revocation of 1685, emigrated to Norwich, Spitalfields, Holland and Brandenburg.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the state that believes it can take a man's religion and keep his trade. Louis XIV revoked the Edict, forbade emigration on pain of the galleys, and expected the Huguenot weavers of Rouen to attend mass and go on weaving; perhaps two hundred thousand left the kingdom, and the skills left with them. The dictionary records this not as a providential joke but as the plain working of a moral order: a crown that treats conscience as a commodity will find that it has valued the commodity wrongly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of a trade pursued as a calling, which is what these congregations were made of. Paul lodged with Aquila and Priscilla and worked, “for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3), and the apostolic charge to a congregation of artisans is to “work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11). What happened to Rouen is what happened at Jerusalem, that after a great persecution “they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1), and the scattered “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch” (Act 11:19), which for Normans meant Norwich, London and Berlin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek skenopoios (G4635), a tentmaker; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; Greek techne (G5078), a trade, an art.

expand to see more

Greek skenopoios (G4635) — a tentmaker; “for by their occupation they were tentmakers”, Acts 18:3.

Greek techne (G5078) — an art, a trade, a craft; “because he was of the same craft”, Acts 18:3.

Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; “and to work with your own hands”, 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad; “they were all scattered abroad”, Acts 8:1.

Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to pass through, to travel; “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch”, Acts 11:19.

Usage

"“for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3) — a congregation of dyers, weavers and printers."

"“they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1) — the Revocation of 1685 and emigration on pain of the galleys."

"“and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — the looms of Norwich and Spitalfields."
